Lifted State Policy Optimization: Internalizing Self-Correction through Transition Geometry

Ren Zhuang    Ben Wang    Shuifa Sun Hangzhou Normal University venomrko97@gmail.com, {20170056, watersun}@hznu.edu.cn
Abstract

Preference optimization ranks final answers and trajectory RL maximizes aggregate returns, yet neither credits the local change that turns a flawed reasoning state into a better one. We introduce Lifted State Policy Optimization (LSPO), which establishes this finite, cost-adjusted transition as the primary unit of learning. Each textual answer is augmented with a learned continuous coordinate, forming a lifted state that an energy function evaluates and orders. A shaped reward drives energy descent net of edit and step costs, and an internalization loss absorbs selected low-energy answers into the direct generator. On Qwen3.5-27B, the resulting single-pass policy reaches 71.8% aggregate accuracy across mathematics, science, code, and logic benchmarks, matching test-time reflection at 71.9% with 28% lower latency and 25.8% fewer tokens. The pattern holds across dense and mixture-of-experts backbones, and matched controls confirm that transition credit and the lifted coordinate each contribute, as does answer internalization. Our code is available at https://github.com/Venomrko/lspo.

1 Introduction

Even strong language models make local mistakes within otherwise sound reasoning, and one faulty step can invalidate the final answer (Uesato et al., 2022; Lightman et al., 2023). Inference methods address this through chain of thought, self-consistency, critique, and repeated refinement (Wei et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023), and large reasoning models extend deliberation into long trajectories (Shao et al., 2024; Zelikman et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). These procedures improve difficult answers, but their gains require additional sampling budgets or persistent refinement loops at deployment. Training can absorb useful corrections into the policy itself, removing this cost.

A central question is defining the appropriate unit of supervision. Current objectives provide supervision at coarse granularity; preference optimization ranks complete outputs (Rafailov et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2024; Meng et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025b), trajectory RL maximizes aggregate returns over full rollouts (Ouyang et al., 2022; Schulman et al., 2017), and self-correction methods learn from entire refinement traces (Kumar et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2025). Each focuses on endpoints or full trajectories, leaving the local transition that resolves a flawed reasoning state as an unmodeled unit of credit. We formalize this gap through transition credit, where the unit of learning is a finite state transition, evaluated by the decrease in a learned energy function net of edit and step costs (Sutton et al., 1998; Kaufmann et al., 2024; Lambert, 2025).

We introduce Lifted State Policy Optimization (LSPO). LSPO augments the textual answer xx with a continuous coordinate zz, forming a lifted state s=(x,z)s=(x,z) that carries refinement context beyond discrete surface text. An energy function E~​(s,q)\tilde{E}(s;q) orders candidate states; a shaped reward favors transitions that decrease energy net of edit and step costs; and an internalization loss trains the generator to produce selected low-energy answers directly from the original input.

We evaluate LSPO across the Qwen3.5 family (Qwen Team, 2026) on mathematics (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Zhang and Math-AI, 2025), science (Rein et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024), executable code (Jain et al., 2024), and logic (Lin et al., 2025). On Qwen3.5-27B, the single-pass policy reaches 71.8% aggregate accuracy, matching test-time reflection at 71.9% with 28% lower latency and 25.8% fewer tokens. The pattern holds across scales, reaching 60.8% at 9B and 72.6% on the 35B-A3B mixture-of-experts backbone. At the mechanism level, as reported in Figure 1, LSPO converts 6.4% of incorrect answers to correct while regressing only 1.7%, yielding a 4.7-point net transition gain.

Our core contributions are threefold.

  • •

    Single-pass reliability. Absorbing selected low-energy endpoints relocates deliberation from inference into training; the deployed policy reaches reflective accuracy in a single pass, across dense and mixture-of-experts backbones.

  • •

    Cost-adjusted transition credit. LSPO establishes a finite state transition as the primary unit of learning, scored by energy decrease net of edit and step costs. Unlike a step-level score, this quantity is relative to a prompt’s candidate pool, steering policy movement rather than global state ranking. Bounded energy error perturbs cumulative credit only through the endpoints, and removing the progress reward costs more net gain than removing any other component.

  • •

    Lifting as refinement context. A learned continuous coordinate carries information about constructive transitions that surface text alone does not; probes on held-out transitions show higher action prediction and energy ranking, while shuffled or zeroed coordinates eliminate this advantage.

2 Method

2.1 Overview

LSPO learns local directions of improvement in a lifted state space and transfers selected answers into a direct policy. It combines a continuous coordinate for refinement context, an energy objective for crediting finite state changes, and an internalization loss that trains the generator on selected answers. Figure 2 contrasts this localized mechanism with paradigms centered on terminal answers or aggregate returns.

2.2 Lifted State

Standard optimization procedures target a distribution pθ​(y∣q)p_{\theta}(y\mid q) over complete outputs for a given input qq, masking the intermediate dynamics of local revisions. To expose these dynamics for training, we cast local improvement as a Markov decision process in an augmented state space. We define a lifted state

st=(xt,zt),s_{t}=(x_{t},z_{t}), (1)

where xtx_{t} represents the surface text and ztz_{t} is a continuous auxiliary coordinate. The auxiliary coordinate is initialized from the input and current answer, updated by the transition block, and projected away when the final answer is written back into text.

We introduce an energy function

E~​(st,q)=E~​(xt,zt,q),\tilde{E}(s_{t};q)=\tilde{E}(x_{t},z_{t};q), (2)

to evaluate state quality. The energy head orders candidate states and defines which answer becomes the target for direct generation. The policy induces a transition distribution Pθ​(st+1∣st,at,q)P_{\theta}(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a_{t},q). Training optimizes the action policy πθ​(at∣st,q)\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t},q) to favor short sequences whose transitions reduce energy.

Because surface text is discrete, moves are finite and are evaluated within visited neighborhoods.

2.3 Training Procedure

The training phase constructs short moves in the lifted state space. At each step, the policy samples an action at∈{revise,switch,stop}a_{t}\in\{\text{revise},\text{switch},\text{stop}\} from πθ​(at∣st,q)\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t},q) to modify the surface text, move the auxiliary coordinate toward an alternative refinement mode, or halt within the current local basin. The frozen projection initializes z0z_{0}; Revise recursively updates ztz_{t}, and Switch resets ztz_{t} before a residual update. The primary configuration uses dz=8d_{z}=8, and the energy head scores the resulting state. The resulting sequence is τ=(s0,a0,s1,a1,…,sT)\tau=(s_{0},a_{0},s_{1},a_{1},\dots,s_{T}). Appendix C defines the edit metric, rollout collection, advantage estimator, and complete training procedure.

2.4 Energy Model and Selection

The energy model establishes an ordering over candidate states that guides both local transitions and final answer selection. It operates as a scalar head over (q,xt,zt)(q,x_{t},z_{t}), shared across training families and fitted on sampled states. Gold answers and executable checkers provide scalar supervision. Verified candidates receive lower energy than unsuccessful ones, with ties broken by shorter edit distance and lower step cost. Pairs are formed within each prompt’s candidate rollouts, assigning lower energy to verified states than to failed or perturbed alternatives.

Selection uses the same object. The generated sequence induces a candidate set 𝒞⁡(q)\mathcal{C}(q) containing the direct answer state and its successors. The method selects the state with the lowest energy

s∗​(q)=arg⁡mins∈𝒞⁡(q)​E~​(s,q)s^{*}(q)=\arg\min_{s\in\mathcal{C}(q)}\tilde{E}(s;q) (3)

and sets xT∗​(q)x_{T}^{*}(q) to be its surface text component as the transfer target. The model is trained to emit xT∗​(q)x_{T}^{*}(q) from the original input. Before policy training, we fit and freeze the entire scoring branch, encompassing the text encoder, lift projection, transition block, and energy head, as detailed in Appendix C.

2.5 Objective

The LSPO objective unifies shaped reinforcement learning over intermediate transitions with answer internalization. The reward for stepwise progress is formulated as

rt=E~​(st,q)−E~​(st+1,q)−λedit​d​(xt+1,xt)−λstep,r_{t}=\tilde{E}(s_{t};q)-\tilde{E}(s_{t+1};q)-\lambda_{\mathrm{edit}}d(x_{t+1},x_{t})-\lambda_{\mathrm{step}}, (4)

for Revise and Switch. Stop preserves the current state and yields zero reward. Here dd penalizes surface edits and λstep\lambda_{\mathrm{step}} regularizes trajectory length. We index the TT text-changing moves by t=0,…,T−1t=0,\ldots,T-1; an optional final Stop contributes zero to their sum.

Proposition 1 (Telescoping Trajectory Reward).

For an input qq and a finite trajectory τ=(s0,a0,…,sT)\tau=(s_{0},a_{0},\dots,s_{T}), the cumulative shaped reward R⁡(τ,q)=∑t=0T−1rtR(\tau;q)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}r_{t} satisfies

R⁡(τ,q)=E~​(s0,q)−E~​(sT,q)−λedit​∑t=0T−1d⁡(xt+1,xt)−λstep​T.R(\tau;q)=\tilde{E}(s_{0};q)-\tilde{E}(s_{T};q)-\lambda_{\mathrm{edit}}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}d(x_{t+1},x_{t})-\lambda_{\mathrm{step}}T. (5)

Because intermediate energy terms telescope, cumulative return reflects net endpoint improvement minus total accrued penalties. The proof appears in Appendix C.

The same telescoping structure provides robustness to scoring error. When training energy differs from E~\tilde{E} by at most ε\varepsilon at visited states, cumulative reward shifts by at most 2​ε2\varepsilon through the endpoints alone, preserving the ranking of trajectories separated by more than 2​ε2\varepsilon, as established in Proposition 4 and Corollary 2.

At update kk, the rollout snapshot θ¯k\bar{\theta}_{k} fixes the initial-state distribution ρθ¯k\rho_{\bar{\theta}_{k}} and text-proposal kernel Kθ¯kK_{\bar{\theta}_{k}}. Controller RL uses the per-update objective

Jctrl(k)(θ)=𝔼τ∼Pρθ¯k,πθ,Kθ¯k[∑trt−β∑tDKL(πθ(⋅∣st,q)∥πref(⋅∣st,q))],J_{\mathrm{ctrl}}^{(k)}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim P_{\rho_{\bar{\theta}_{k}},\pi_{\theta},K_{\bar{\theta}_{k}}}}\Big[\sum_{t}r_{t}-\beta\sum_{t}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t},q)\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{t},q)\right)\Big], (6)

where the action KL includes Stop. The initialization and proposal mechanisms are held fixed within an update and refreshed for the next one. The visited-state KL follows regularized policy optimization (Schulman et al., 2015; Schulman et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2025).

To absorb the selected improvements into the generator, we incorporate a loss for selected internalization

JSI​(θ)=𝔼q​[log⁡pθ​(xT∗​(q)∣q)],J_{\mathrm{SI}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{q}\left[\log p_{\theta}(x_{T}^{*}(q)\mid q)\right], (7)

where xT∗​(q)x_{T}^{*}(q) denotes the selected final output with the lowest energy produced during the alignment phase. The final objective is

JLSPO(k)​(θ)=Jctrl(k)​(θ)+α​JSI​(θ).J_{\mathrm{LSPO}}^{(k)}(\theta)=J_{\mathrm{ctrl}}^{(k)}(\theta)+\alpha J_{\mathrm{SI}}(\theta). (8)

Task feedback supplies the supervision used to fit the energy ordering.

Formal properties of the objective appear in the appendices. In particular, the internalization loss corresponds to a forward KL projection onto the selected answer distribution in Appendix D, while Appendix A gives a path-distribution relaxation and an information criterion for useful lifting.

At deployment, the compiled conditional distribution serves each answer through direct generation, requiring no auxiliary lifted-state computation during inference.

3 Experiments

We investigate whether geometry-inspired transition credit produces reliable direct reasoning. The main text tests answer quality, preservation of correct states, deployment cost, component contributions, and training dynamics; benchmark-level held-out evaluations and supplemental transfer tests appear in Appendix E.

3.1 Protocol

Models.

We evaluate LSPO across the Qwen3.5 family (Qwen Team, 2026) to assess scaling dynamics. Qwen3.5-27B is the primary model for component and mechanism analysis; Qwen3.5-35B-A3B supplies transfer evidence for the mixture-of-experts setting alongside its architectural ablation. We also include reference metrics from gpt-oss-120b (OpenAI, 2025) and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (Anthropic, 2025).

Benchmarks.

The evaluation spans six suites covering MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021), AIME25 (Zhang and Math-AI, 2025), GPQA (Rein et al., 2024), LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2024), ZebraLogic (Lin et al., 2025), and MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024). Code tasks measure execution validity through pass@kk evaluation (Chen et al., 2021). We additionally incorporate GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), ARC-Challenge (Clark et al., 2018), BBH (Suzgun et al., 2023), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) to assess transfer to task families outside the training distribution.

Baselines.

We compare LSPO against several baselines, including the preference optimization methods DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) and Step-DPO (Lai et al., 2024), the RL approaches GRPO (Guo et al., 2025) and GDPO (Panaganti et al., 2026), and SCoRe (Kumar et al., 2024), a self-correction method that learns directly from revision traces generated by the model. Matched training alternatives for candidate selection, answer internalization, coordinate controls, and test-time reflection complement these primary baselines.

Implementation Details.

All primary comparisons use fixed configurations across random seeds 42, 1234, and 3407. The primary runs use short training sequences with Tmax=6T_{\max}=6, top-pp 0.95, an 8-dimensional auxiliary lift dz=8d_{z}=8, and an internalization weight of 0.3. Appendix C details optimizers, sampling parameters, sweep ranges, matched training alternatives, and extended analyses. The deployment comparison reports direct pass@1 generation for LSPO alongside an iterative reflection baseline evaluated with two inference passes under identical seeds and settings. Training targets use verifiers and search; the deployment comparison samples from the trained conditional model.

3.2 Main Results

Overall Performance.

Table 1 reports direct pass@1 accuracy across six benchmark suites. LSPO achieves the highest aggregate accuracy among direct-generation baselines on each Qwen3.5 backbone, with the largest margins on structured reasoning tasks, including MATH-500, AIME25, ZebraLogic, and LiveCodeBench, where local intermediate state transitions crucially govern final outcomes. On the knowledge-oriented GPQA and MMLU-Pro benchmarks, LSPO improves over the base model while maintaining a compact direct-generation profile. The pattern holds across all three backbones in Appendix B, with the largest improvements at 9B and 27B where exploration has more headroom to reshape generation.

Deployment Efficiency.

Figure 3 shows the LSPO policy reaching 71.8% aggregate accuracy with 10.93 s average latency and 1265 output tokens. It remains above the pass@kk curve across sampled budgets and executes the highest volume of constructive edits. Test-time reflection reaches 71.9% with 15.18 s and 1705 tokens across two inference passes. LSPO thus achieves comparable observed accuracy in a single pass with 4.25 s lower latency and 440 fewer tokens per answer, serving each answer directly through the compiled generator.

3.3 Mechanism Analyses

Preserving Improvements.

Table 2 measures whether policies retain improvements found along training paths while protecting correct states. Over the same paired-answer denominator, LSPO repairs 6.4% and damages 1.7% of answers, yielding a 4.7-point net gain. It records the lowest direct energy of 0.3980.398 and terminal energy of 0.1950.195 among methods with an energy head; the terminal value bounds exploration capacity during training, while the direct value measures whether improvements are internalized into the policy. The span audit preserves 95.8% of initially valid spans and yields a 16.0-point net validity gain as detailed in Appendix D.

Sources of Improvement.

Table 3 separates gains from target selection and internalization from those of the full LSPO objective, then compares the resulting policy with test-time reflection at deployment. LSPO exceeds Select then SFT and selected internalization, listed as SI only in the table, by 1.2 and 1.0 aggregate points, respectively. This reflection baseline reaches comparable accuracy at 71.9% while incurring substantially higher deployment overhead, requiring two inference passes that add 4.25 s latency and 440 tokens per query.

Generalization Across Task Families.

Direct generation and frozen energy ordering are evaluated on five benchmark suites held out from policy training, energy fitting, and endpoint selection in Appendix E. LSPO improves over Base on every held-out benchmark and reaches an average of 74.9, above SCoRe at 74.3. The frozen energy model also preserves local candidate ordering on this benchmark-level holdout, showing that the learned state signal remains useful on task families excluded from fitting and endpoint selection.

Training Dynamics.

Figure 4 tracks the learning phases. Transition stability and net gain rise rapidly in the early steps, marking the formation of a geometric landscape before the accuracy curve plateaus. LSPO first stabilizes constructive local moves and then converts this geometry into deployed accuracy. In contrast, SCoRe trains on unconstrained self-revision traces without step penalties, which leads to aggressive rewriting of correct spans and higher C→\toW degradation, regressing initially correct answers into erroneous states. LSPO avoids this failure mode by bounding the revision scope throughout training.

Component Ablations.

Table 4 isolates each core mechanism. Removing the lifted coordinate reduces aggregate quality and net transition gain, while dropping the progress reward lowers net gain and inflates output verbosity. Removing answer internalization degrades retention and lowers aggregate accuracy. Parameter-matched coordinate controls retain the same training budget yet remain 0.9–1.5 aggregate points below full LSPO, supporting a role for learned refinement context beyond parameter count alone. The full LSPO stack requires additional training compute, while its structural constraints reduce deployment latency and token count relative to unshaped RL baselines. Appendix C provides the coordinate controls, matched training alternatives, and the full MoE ablation.

Policy Energy and Task-Level Gains.

Figure 5 tracks recorded energy across policy updates alongside task-level correction outcomes. Energy decreases rapidly during early training and then approaches a plateau, with fluctuations between updates. The cumulative minimum curve records the lowest energy observed across updates, with highlighted points marking new minima. The right panel reports benchmark-level net correction gains independently, with LSPO showing negative net gain on MATH-500 and positive net gains on the other five benchmarks.

4 Discussion

Scope and Boundaries of Local Correction.

The transition audits show positive net correction gains on five of six benchmarks, with MATH-500 marking an operational boundary for test-time revision. In tightly coupled algebraic derivations, modifying an isolated step without revising preceding assertions leaves upstream inconsistencies that cause test-time perturbations to degrade more answers than they repair across all methods. As illustrated in Appendix F on AIME25, resolution requires rebuilding from an alternative decomposition beyond finite-radius edits. In this regime, LSPO internalizes and preserves valid proof structures; training on low-energy trajectories commits coherent derivations to the generator, allowing direct accuracy in Table 1 to advance even where test-time trajectory gain does not. Removing internalization costs 1.5 aggregate points and degrades correct-span retention, confirming that the generator drives this gain.

Prior analyses of iterative self-correction (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2025) describe the same distinction. Local correction repairs errors that represent isolated adjustments within a sound plan, including sign choices, index offsets, and lemma applications. Conversely, when the overarching plan requires fundamental restructuring, local energy gradients offer no direct descent toward the target answer. Traversing such global transitions requires either test-time search or training curricula that expose the policy to plan-level pivots.

Training Cost and Deployment Trade-offs.

LSPO invests 2983 GPU-hours during training to yield per-query reductions of 4.25 s in latency and 440 output tokens at deployment. The return on this compute investment scales with serving volume, where low-throughput regimes favor minimal training overhead, while high-throughput serving amortizes it through cumulative per-query latency and token savings.

This compute allocation also differs qualitatively from test-time scaling. Reflection-based methods (Snell et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Sun, 2026) let a single checkpoint serve both simple and complex queries by dynamically varying inference compute. In contrast, LSPO compiles deliberation directly into network parameters, producing a faster single-pass deployment where each query incurs identical inference cost regardless of difficulty. Hybrid designs that use LSPO as a fast initial pass and fall back to explicit search on high-energy outputs could combine the advantages of both regimes.

Representational Role of the Lifted Coordinate.

Frozen probing evaluations demonstrate that appending the learned coordinate zz to textual representations improves action prediction and energy ranking on held-out transitions in Table C.8, whereas prompt-shuffled controls degrade performance, confirming that the coordinate carries prompt-specific information inaccessible to a text predictor. Architecturally, the coordinate can encode compressed revision histories reflecting edit count and convergence, or establish distinct neighborhoods through Switch to identify candidate answer basins, both of which match empirical observations.

The learned coordinate guides local trajectory steps within candidate vicinities. As shown by the selection-budget analysis in Appendix E, energy-based ranking discriminates reliably across moderate candidate neighborhoods, whereas unconstrained candidate expansion encounters non-convex surface irregularities. The lifted coordinate thereby provides directionality along local improvement paths, guiding policy updates without assuming global convexity.

5 Related Work

Final Answers, Steps, and Trajectories.

Outcome supervision and preference learning supply signals over final answers through RLHF (Christiano et al., 2017; Ziegler et al., 2019; Stiennon et al., 2020), constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022), and direct optimization objectives (Rafailov et al., 2023). ORPO (Hong et al., 2024), SimPO (Meng et al., 2024), and rewards generated by the model (Yuan et al., 2024) refine this interface for ranking answers (Liu et al., 2025b). Process supervision moves the learning signal into intermediate reasoning steps (Cobbe et al., 2021; Uesato et al., 2022; Lightman et al., 2023), with Step-DPO as a prominent example (Lai et al., 2024). Unlike absolute step scores suited to reranking individual states, LSPO credits relative transitions net of edit and step costs within a prompt’s candidate pool, steering policy movement rather than global state ranking. GRPO (Guo et al., 2025) and GDPO (Panaganti et al., 2026) optimize returns over sampled trajectories.

Learning from Refinement.

Refinement during inference enables models to critique, revise, or retry initial answers (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023; Sun, 2026). Recent training variants convert these revisions into supervision through rewards generated by the model, revision analysis, and refinement pipelines for code (Liu et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2025; Bensal et al., 2025; Xiong et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2026). SCoRe is the closest baseline, learning from refinement traces generated by the model (Kumar et al., 2024).

Representing Intermediate States.

State representation determines which movements can be compared and optimized. Plain text exposes the current answer but confines candidate alternatives to a brittle discrete space. Calibration and semantic-uncertainty studies show that confidence and correctness signals reside on separable manifolds in the hidden state (Guo et al., 2017; Kuhn et al., 2023; Farquhar et al., 2024); semantic probes and over-confidence analyses further confirm that correctness structure is geometrically accessible (Kossen et al., 2024; Morosini et al., 2026). Complementary geometric methods treat latent representations as substrates for reasoning and model connectivity (Xie et al., 2025; Zhuang et al., 2026). LSPO operationalizes this view by lifting surface answers into an augmented state space, ordering candidate transitions by energy, and transferring the selected lower-energy answer into direct generation.

6 Limitations and Future Directions

The framework is designed for verifiable reasoning tasks where programmatic checkers or scalar outcomes ground the energy landscape. Policy improvement relies on alignment between the learned energy E~​(s,q)\tilde{E}(s;q) and true answer validity. While intermediate fluctuations cancel telescopically along trajectories, terminal discrimination remains bounded by the fidelity of the fitted scoring head. Operating over visited neighborhoods, transition credit addresses local repairs within an established derivation, while problems requiring global proof reformulations from scratch remain outside this local search scope. Trajectory exploration concentrates compute during training, making the framework most advantageous for high-throughput serving environments where amortized efficiency provides operational gains.

Our analysis evaluates scaling across the Qwen3.5 family (Qwen Team, 2026), the 35B-A3B mixture-of-experts backbone, and cross-family transfer on Gemma-4-E4B-it (Google DeepMind, 2026). In this work, the auxiliary coordinate models textual deliberation; incorporating tool executions, evidence graphs, or multi-turn interaction traces would define the corresponding state representation for structured environments. Preliminary evaluations in Appendix E show positive policy transfer on open-form writing and roleplay benchmarks, with geometric ordering aligning best with instruction fit, coherence, and character consistency. More comprehensive open-ended creative tasks remain to be evaluated under distinct criteria. Further advances will require latent state spaces that score and retain structured movements across these varied task formats.

7 Conclusion

LSPO establishes that direct policy execution can attain the reliability of iterative refinement. It matches the accuracy of test-time reflection in a single pass, and transition diagnostics confirm that the policy repairs incorrect states while preserving correct ones. The learned stopping behavior mitigates redundant revisions, and the policy transfers across model scales, to held-out benchmarks, and to mixture-of-experts architectures. Attributing credit to geometric transitions and internalizing selected endpoints thus relocates deliberation from inference into the deployed policy.
