Appendices

The appendix follows the evidential order of the main text. It first fixes the formal objects used by LSPO, then tests scale and transfer, isolates training mechanisms, audits internalization and energy ordering, and closes with cases that mark the method boundary.

  • •

    Appendix A derives the path form with KL regularization and the information criterion for lifted states.

  • •

    Appendix B reports scale and transfer across Qwen sizes, benchmark families, and a distinct Gemma backbone.

  • •

    Appendix C connects the update contract to component ablations, sensitivity analyses, and the fixed training configuration.

  • •

    Appendix D audits alignment from training to direct generation, stopping behavior, and the boundary with test-time reflection.

  • •

    Appendix E quantifies deployment cost, energy ordering on benchmark suites held out from training, and compute accounting.

  • •

    Appendix F maps the mechanism onto representative repairs and a global search failure case.

Appendix A Formal Properties of the Path Objective and State Lifting

This appendix studies an unrestricted path-distribution relaxation and an information criterion for lifting. Their conclusions concern the stated distributions and assumptions.

Proposition 2 (Gibbs form of the path optimizer constrained by KL divergence).

Fix a prompt qq, let Pref(⋅∣q)P_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid q) be a reference distribution over finite correction trajectories, and define the path score

Fq​(τ)=∑t=0T⁡(τ)−1rt.F_{q}(\tau)=\sum_{t=0}^{T(\tau)-1}r_{t}. (A.1)

Consider the variational problem

supP≪Pref(⋅∣q){𝔼τ∼P[Fq(τ)]−βDKL(P∥Pref(⋅∣q))}.\sup_{P\ll P_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid q)}\left\{\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim P}[F_{q}(\tau)]-\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(P\,\|\,P_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid q)\big)\right\}. (A.2)

For β>0\beta>0 and 0<Zq<∞0<Z_{q}<\infty, its unique maximizer is the exponentially tilted path distribution

d​Pq⋆d​Pref(τ)=exp⁡(Fq​(τ)/β)Zq,Zq=𝔼τ∼Pref(⋅∣q)[exp(Fq(τ)/β)],\frac{dP_{q}^{\star}}{dP_{\mathrm{ref}}}(\tau)=\frac{\exp(F_{q}(\tau)/\beta)}{Z_{q}},\hskip 18.49988ptZ_{q}=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim P_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid q)}\left[\exp(F_{q}(\tau)/\beta)\right], (A.3)

and the optimal objective value equals β​log⁡Zq\beta\log Z_{q}.

Variational argument.

Let Pq⋆P_{q}^{\star} be the tilted path distribution defined in eq. A.3. For any admissible PP, we have

d​Pq⋆d​Pref​(τ)=exp⁡(Fq​(τ)/β)Zq.\frac{dP_{q}^{\star}}{dP_{\mathrm{ref}}}(\tau)=\frac{\exp(F_{q}(\tau)/\beta)}{Z_{q}}. (A.4)

This gives

log⁡d​Pq⋆d​Pref​(τ)=Fq​(τ)β−log⁡Zq.\log\frac{dP_{q}^{\star}}{dP_{\mathrm{ref}}}(\tau)=\frac{F_{q}(\tau)}{\beta}-\log Z_{q}. (A.5)

Using

DKL(P∥Pq⋆)=𝔼τ∼P[logd​Pd​Pq⋆(τ)]=𝔼τ∼P[logd​Pd​Pref(τ)−Fq​(τ)β+logZq],D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\,\|\,P_{q}^{\star})=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim P}\left[\log\frac{dP}{dP_{q}^{\star}}(\tau)\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim P}\left[\log\frac{dP}{dP_{\mathrm{ref}}}(\tau)-\frac{F_{q}(\tau)}{\beta}+\log Z_{q}\right], (A.6)

we rearrange to obtain

𝔼τ∼P[Fq(τ)]−βDKL(P∥Pref(⋅∣q))=βlogZq−βDKL(P∥Pq⋆).\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim P}[F_{q}(\tau)]-\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(P\,\|\,P_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid q)\big)=\beta\log Z_{q}-\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\,\|\,P_{q}^{\star}). (A.7)

The right side is maximized uniquely at P=Pq⋆P=P_{q}^{\star}, where the KL term vanishes.

Path Variational Form.

Proposition 2 casts the path problem with a KL constraint as a variational optimization whose solution tilts the reference distribution toward paths with larger cumulative progress. Together with proposition 1, the result places lower final energy, edit cost, and step cost within a single path preference.

Relation to the Implemented Regularizer.

For a fixed prompt, a policy-induced path distribution factors as

Pθ​(τ∣q)=ρθ​(s0∣q)​∏tπθ​(at∣st,q)​Kθ​(st+1∣st,at,q),P_{\theta}(\tau\mid q)=\rho_{\theta}(s_{0}\mid q)\prod_{t}\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t},q)K_{\theta}(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a_{t},q), (A.8)

including the Stop decision and absorbing termination. Under absolute continuity, the chain rule gives

DKL(Pθ∥Pref)=\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{\theta}\|P_{\mathrm{ref}})={} DKL(ρθ∥ρref)\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\rho_{\theta}\|\rho_{\mathrm{ref}}) (A.9)
+𝔼Pθ∑tDKL(πθ(⋅∣st,q)∥πref(⋅∣st,q))\displaystyle+\mathbb{E}_{P_{\theta}}\sum_{t}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t},q)\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{t},q))
+𝔼Pθ∑tDKL(Kθ(⋅∣st,at,q)∥Kref(⋅∣st,at,q)).\displaystyle+\mathbb{E}_{P_{\theta}}\sum_{t}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(K_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t},q)\|K_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t},q)).

Equality with the action-KL term requires shared initial-state distributions and conditional transition kernels. Within update kk, LSPO fixes ρθ¯k\rho_{\bar{\theta}_{k}} and Kθ¯kK_{\bar{\theta}_{k}} for both the controller and the reference, whereby the first and third terms above cancel and the path KL reduces to the visited-state action KL. Controller RL therefore targets the fixed-mechanism controller objective in eq. 6 rather than the unrestricted path objective; the snapshot is refreshed at the next update. The Gibbs result concerns the unrestricted path-distribution relaxation, whose optimum further requires realizability under the specified dynamics.

A.1 Information in the Lifted State

The lifted coordinate ztz_{t} augments the discrete textual state. Whether lifting adds value depends on the information it carries about constructive moves beyond what the surface text and prompt alone provide.

Proposition 3 (Lifted state reduces optimal move prediction loss by the conditional mutual information).

Let UtU_{t} denote any target associated with state sts_{t}, for example an indicator that a candidate local move decreases energy without harming correctness. Define the Bayes optimal predictors

psurf⋆​(u∣x,q)=ℙ⁡(Ut=u∣Xt=x,Q=q)p^{\star}_{\mathrm{surf}}(u\mid x,q)=\mathbb{P}(U_{t}=u\mid X_{t}=x,Q=q) (A.10)

and

plift⋆​(u∣x,z,q)=ℙ⁡(Ut=u∣Xt=x,Zt=z,Q=q).p^{\star}_{\mathrm{lift}}(u\mid x,z,q)=\mathbb{P}(U_{t}=u\mid X_{t}=x,Z_{t}=z,Q=q). (A.11)

The achievable reduction in log loss from using the lifted state instead of the surface state alone is

𝔼[−logpsurf⋆(Ut∣Xt,Q)]−𝔼[−logplift⋆(Ut∣Xt,Zt,Q)]=I(Ut;Zt∣Xt,Q).\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\log p^{\star}_{\mathrm{surf}}(U_{t}\mid X_{t},Q)\right]-\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\log p^{\star}_{\mathrm{lift}}(U_{t}\mid X_{t},Z_{t},Q)\right]=I(U_{t};Z_{t}\mid X_{t},Q). (A.12)

Information identity.

By the definition of Bayes optimal log loss,

𝔼⁡[−log⁡psurf⋆​(Ut∣Xt,Q)]=H⁡(Ut∣Xt,Q)\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\log p^{\star}_{\mathrm{surf}}(U_{t}\mid X_{t},Q)\right]=H(U_{t}\mid X_{t},Q) (A.13)

and

𝔼⁡[−log⁡plift⋆​(Ut∣Xt,Zt,Q)]=H⁡(Ut∣Xt,Zt,Q).\mathbb{E}\!\left[-\log p^{\star}_{\mathrm{lift}}(U_{t}\mid X_{t},Z_{t},Q)\right]=H(U_{t}\mid X_{t},Z_{t},Q). (A.14)

Subtracting yields

H(Ut∣Xt,Q)−H(Ut∣Xt,Zt,Q)=I(Ut;Zt∣Xt,Q).H(U_{t}\mid X_{t},Q)-H(U_{t}\mid X_{t},Z_{t},Q)=I(U_{t};Z_{t}\mid X_{t},Q). (A.15)

This is the conditional mutual information identity.

Lift Criterion.

For a fixed joint distribution of (Q,Xt,Zt,Ut)(Q,X_{t},Z_{t},U_{t}) with finite conditional entropies, the identity yields an information criterion. The lifted coordinate ztz_{t} improves prediction exactly when it carries information about constructive moves absent from the surface text and input. Positive conditional mutual information equals the achievable reduction in optimal log loss.

For a deterministic reprojection Zt=g⁡(Q,Xt)Z_{t}=g(Q,X_{t}) at fixed parameters, the conditional mutual information is zero. Recursive coordinates can retain history since their most recent reset; positive conditional information depends on the resulting state distribution and target UtU_{t}. The finite-capacity probes quantify accessible predictive information, and their NLL differences give empirical prediction gains.

Appendix B Full Scaling Profiles and Cross-Architecture Transfer

This appendix extends the 27B analysis across benchmarks, model scales, and pass@kk budgets. Following established protocols for reasoning and executable code evaluation [Wang et al., 2022, Chen et al., 2021], it reports performance for each benchmark across all three Qwen backbones.

Across scales, LSPO attains the highest direct accuracy without collapsing the pass@16 envelope, while expanding sampled ceilings on complex reasoning suites, as illustrated in Figures B.1, B.2 and B.3. The separation is largest on MATH-500, GPQA, and ZebraLogic, where methods based on preferences capture less of the available revision signal than on broad knowledge tasks. Smaller models retain wider gaps between pass@1 and pass@16, indicating more residual search headroom.

These distributions relate LSPO to recent reasoning systems operating at scale, such as DeepSeekMath and DeepSeek-R1 [Shao et al., 2024, Guo et al., 2025]. Reasoning RL at large scale can improve quality by reshaping output distributions and spending inference compute. The pass@16 diagnostics isolate the portion of that improvement absorbed into deployed generation while sampled diversity remains available.

B.1 Transfer Across Backbones

While primary scaling experiments evaluate the Qwen3.5 family under consistent formatting, Table B.1 examines transfer to Gemma-4-E4B-it [Google DeepMind, 2026]. On this distinct backbone, LSPO attains the highest aggregate score, improving over both offline preference optimization and online reinforcement learning with only a modest latency increase. This confirms that transition credit and answer internalization transfer robustly beyond the primary Qwen family.

B.2 Benchmark Coverage

The benchmark suite spans complementary reasoning regimes. MATH-500 and AIME assess multi-step mathematical derivations. LiveCodeBench tests executable code synthesis under formal test specifications. ZebraLogic probes constrained deduction and local backtrack revisions. GPQA and MMLU-Pro assess multi-step scientific and domain knowledge. In addition, held-out task suites such as BBH, GSM8K, and HumanEval are evaluated in Appendix E to audit out-of-distribution calibration.

Appendix C Update Mechanics, Ablations, and Sensitivity Analyses

This appendix links the training procedure to the mechanisms tested in the main text. The three core mechanisms of LSPO play complementary roles. Lifting defines the state in which correction moves are compared; the progress reward supplies dense local credit, aligned with reward shaping and process supervision [Ng et al., 1999, Uesato et al., 2022, Lightman et al., 2023]; and answer internalization moves selected candidates into the deployed policy.

Baseline comparisons place LSPO mechanics against neighboring training strategies. Step-DPO [Lai et al., 2024] strengthens supervision over long reasoning chains relative to standard DPO while retaining a preference objective. GDPO [Panaganti et al., 2026] addresses stability in RL over sampled paths through group weighting. SCoRe [Kumar et al., 2024] trains online self-correction from the model’s own generation traces. LSPO combines cost-aware move shaping with answer internalization so that selected states enter generation in a single pass.

The accompanying ablations examine the contributions of state lifting and reward shaping under the reported configurations, complementing studies of shaped training signals in reinforcement learning [Kaufmann et al., 2024, Lambert, 2025, Wu et al., 2026a].

C.1 Update Mechanics

Figure C.1 and Algorithm 1 specify the computational graph and algorithmic procedure for a single LSPO update.

The initial generation at the top of the update graph represents the deployed answer before revision. This output initializes the lifted path and the candidate set. Each state encodes the surface text, the lifted coordinate, and the scalar energy. Each action proposes a local move and receives the reward increment from eq. 4. This decomposition combines credit assignment over paths with direct training on the selected answer. The advantage estimator targets the controller objective in eq. 6.

C.2 Architecture and Data Transparency

The primary Qwen3.5-27B implementation uses the architecture and public corpus mixture in Tables C.1 and C.2. These details fix how the lifted coordinate enters the model, how the energy head receives text and state features, and which data mixture supplies the shared training budget.

Algorithm 1 fixes the training contract. The model generates the deployed answer, explores lifted states during training, selects a candidate, and updates the direct generator on that answer. The energy model, verifier, candidate selection, and explicit revision actions serve as instruments during training only.

Transition Operators.

The action set contains three operators. Revise edits the active surface answer by sampling a bounded patch over a reasoning, equation, or code span and recursively updating its coordinate. Switch replaces the active candidate with another sampled state for the same prompt, including its surface text and projected coordinate, before the transition block applies the residual update. Stop terminates expansion and leaves the current state as a candidate for selection. The edit term d⁡(xt+1,xt)d(x_{t+1},x_{t}) is computed after normalizing whitespace, mathematical tokens, and code tokens. Long answers are segmented into reasoning spans, and the distance is the normalized Levenshtein distance at token level over changed spans, capped at one for each transition. This convention charges local rewrites without making copied context dominate the penalty.

Lifted Coordinate.

Let ht=hξ​(q,xt)h_{t}=h_{\xi}(q,x_{t}) be the frozen text representation and e⁡(at)e(a_{t}) the frozen action embedding used by the transition block. Initialization uses z0=gψ​(h0)z_{0}=g_{\psi}(h_{0}). For Revise, the residual update starts from bt=ztb_{t}=z_{t}; for Switch, it starts from bt=gψ​(ht+1)b_{t}=g_{\psi}(h_{t+1}). Both use

zt+1=LN⁡(bt+fη​(ht+1−ht,bt,e⁡(at))).z_{t+1}=\mathrm{LN}\!\left(b_{t}+f_{\eta}(h_{t+1}-h_{t},b_{t},e(a_{t}))\right). (C.1)

Revise therefore retains refinement history through ztz_{t}, while Switch resets that history to the replacement candidate. Stop preserves ztz_{t}. The energy E~​(st,q)=Eϕ​(ht,zt,q)\tilde{E}(s_{t};q)=E_{\phi}(h_{t},z_{t},q) and action policy πθ(⋅∣st,q)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t},q) consume the same stored coordinate.

Training Stages and Gradient Scope.

We first fit the scoring branch on sampled training states using the energy-ranking supervision described below. Before policy optimization, we freeze the text encoder hξh_{\xi}, projection gψg_{\psi}, transition block fηf_{\eta} (including its conditioning embeddings and normalization), and energy head EϕE_{\phi}. The scoring encoder is a fixed parameter copy, separate from the trainable generator. These components remain fixed throughout rollout collection, candidate selection, RL/SI updates, and ordering audits. Coordinates can evolve recursively even though the update function is frozen.

Within each update, initial answers and text proposals are sampled using the rollout snapshot and treated as fixed environment outcomes for controller RL. Shared parameters receive gradients from both controller RL and answer internalization, which maximizes the likelihood of selected answers given the original prompt. A value-regression loss trains the value head. Rewards, stored scoring features, and selected targets are detached supervision; the ranking loss is confined to scoring-branch fitting. Thus RL/SI gradients leave all scoring-branch parameters unchanged.

Energy Supervision.

Energy supervision is built from comparisons among states visited for the same prompt. Checkers for exact match, executable tests, multiple choice labels, and task verifiers identify successful states. Failed answers, states rejected by verifiers, longer states with no verifier improvement, variants with noisy energy, and controls using terminal rewards only supply negatives. The scalar head is fit with a pairwise margin objective so that verified states or states with lower cost receive lower energy than alternatives from the same prompt. The head is fit on training families, then frozen for candidate selection and for the ordering audit on held-out families in Appendix E; GSM8K, ARC-Challenge, BBH, HumanEval, and MBPP are excluded from fitting and endpoint selection in that audit.

Policy Update.

Rollouts are generated by the current policy for the current minibatch, and no replay buffer carries trajectories across optimizer updates. Advantages are computed from the shaped rewards with generalized advantage estimation using discount γ=1\gamma=1 and λ=0.95\lambda=0.95, followed by normalization and value clipping at 0.20.2. The KL term is evaluated against the fixed reference action policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} on the same visited states. The rollout policy πθ¯k\pi_{\bar{\theta}_{k}} supplies the sampling probabilities for the update and is distinct from this reference. Stop is recorded with zero reward and a terminal mask, giving zero value bootstrap while retaining its policy-gradient and action-KL terms. The finite rollout horizon also terminates the episode with zero bootstrap. Scoring-branch fitting precedes these policy updates.

Action Statistics.

The observed action frequencies in Table C.3 show a shift from exploration toward termination over training. Revise and Switch transitions decrease energy in most executed cases, while the lower probability of reaching TmaxT_{\max} later in training is consistent with the stop action terminating local basins once further movement no longer offsets its costs.

Objective Components.

The flow diagram follows information propagation through the update sequence. Figure C.2 maps each symbolic block to its contribution within that update.

C.3 Objective Context

From a reinforcement learning perspective, LSPO addresses the balance between sparse final rewards, dense shaping signals, and variance control [Sutton et al., 1998]. The progress reward gives the optimizer a local signal over lifted moves rather than raw token sequences, making constructive revisions legible while reducing the burden on credit assigned only to the final answer.

Recent reasoning RL literature reinforces the emphasis on signal structure. Reward design shapes whether policy learning remains stable and semantically aligned [Pan et al., 2026]. The LSPO ablations study the components governing state definition, local improvement criteria, and deployed execution.

Two contemporary research strands reinforce this reading. Transformed objectives improve pass@kk performance within frameworks similar to GRPO [Le et al., 2026], indicating that reasoning RL is sensitive to objective design. Reward model analyses further show that downstream RL depends on accurate preferences and verifiable rationales [Lai et al., 2026]. LSPO applies this lesson to individual moves, where the supervisory signal is shaped by energy descent and edit costs.

C.4 Training Component Analysis

Figure C.3 reports the primary 27B comparison. Test-time reflection reaches 71.9% aggregate accuracy, 0.1 points above LSPO’s 71.8%, while LSPO uses 4.25 s less latency and 440 fewer tokens. GRPO supplies a reinforcement learning comparison over final-answer rewards under the same seed set and sampling budget.

Tables C.4 and C.7 compare LSPO with controlled training alternatives. SI only on a fixed LSPO candidate pool uses the candidates and selected targets produced by Full LSPO, and measures what answer internalization achieves given those teacher candidates. Select then SFT uses the same fixed pool with verifier-based selection and predetermined cost rules. Candidate construction is accounted for separately from the matched SI/SFT token exposure and updates. LSPO leads both alternatives; the paired intervals are positive. These comparisons distinguish downstream training effects conditional on the candidate pool; the teacher pool itself already reflects LSPO exploration.

Return-Matched Terminal Reward.

To isolate reward timing, the terminal control retains the scoring function, edit metric, action space, target selection, termination rules, SI, and action KL of Full LSPO. For a completed trajectory with MM executed Revise/Switch moves and final state sMs_{M}, define

R⁡(τ,q)=E~​(s0,q)−E~​(sM,q)−λedit​∑t=0M−1d⁡(xt+1,xt)−λstep​M.R(\tau;q)=\tilde{E}(s_{0};q)-\tilde{E}(s_{M};q)-\lambda_{\mathrm{edit}}\sum_{t=0}^{M-1}d(x_{t+1},x_{t})-\lambda_{\mathrm{step}}M. (C.2)

Let LL count all recorded decisions, including an explicit Stop when present. The terminal control pays

rtterminal={0,t<L−1,R⁡(τ,q),t=L−1.∑t=0L−1rtterminal=∑t=0L−1rtdense=R⁡(τ,q).r_{t}^{\mathrm{terminal}}=\begin{cases}0,&t<L-1,\\ R(\tau;q),&t=L-1.\end{cases}\hskip 18.49988pt\sum_{t=0}^{L-1}r_{t}^{\mathrm{terminal}}=\sum_{t=0}^{L-1}r_{t}^{\mathrm{dense}}=R(\tau;q). (C.3)

An explicit Stop receives the delayed trajectory return; at the horizon, the last executed move receives it. Immediate Stop gives M=0M=0 and zero return. Full LSPO retains zero reward for Stop itself. With γ=1\gamma=1 and unchanged KL regularization, the two objectives assign the same return to every identical trajectory. Their sampled updates differ through reward timing, value fitting, and GAE with λ=0.95\lambda=0.95, thereby testing finite-sample optimization rather than a different ideal trajectory objective.

Table C.5 extends the ablation analysis. Restricting the policy to paths that only revise degrades both aggregate quality and transition gain, pointing to the role of motion in the lifted state space beyond surface rewriting. Table C.6 measures sensitivity to energy corruption. Gaussian perturbations weaken but preserve part of the transition gain, while flipped or shuffled ordering drives rank metrics toward chance. The terminal reward control retains the trajectory return while delaying its feedback to termination.

C.5 Lifted Coordinate Analysis and MoE Transfer

The frozen probe in Table C.8 tests the predictive utility of zz for a finite-capacity predictor on held-out transitions. Text plus the learned coordinate improves action prediction, reduces NLL, and increases energy AUC; shuffling zz disrupts the prompt association. These probe differences measure predictive utility for the fitted probe; the information identity in Proposition 3 concerns Bayes-optimal log loss.

Table C.9 evaluates whether the lifted-coordinate result is explained by parameter count or generic conditioning capacity. The controls use the same Qwen3.5-27B backbone, candidate budget, training budget, and three-seed protocol as full LSPO. A same-parameter no-lift MLP, a random coordinate, a learned nuisance coordinate, and a frozen or random projection all remain below full LSPO. Their net gains range from 2.8 to 3.0 points, compared with 4.7 for full LSPO; the paired intervals for the aggregate gaps remain positive. These results support the interpretation that the learned, prompt-conditioned coordinate carries refinement-relevant information beyond extra parameters alone.

Table C.10 repeats the component analysis on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. The same ordering of full LSPO over the component removals provides transfer evidence for the MoE backbone, while Qwen3.5-27B remains the setting used for the primary causal comparison.

C.6 Training Configuration

The following configuration specifies the primary training setting and the sensitivity ranges used in the component analyses.

The primary 27B LSPO run follows a fixed configuration. Reported means use seeds 42, 1234, and 3407. The objective coefficients are β=0.02\beta=0.02, λedit=0.10\lambda_{\mathrm{edit}}=0.10, and λstep=0.01\lambda_{\mathrm{step}}=0.01. The environment uses a maximum path length of 6, an auxiliary dimension of 88, an imitation weight of 0.3, temperature 0.6, and top-p=0.95p=0.95. Optimization uses the Muon optimizer across all trainable parameters [Jordan et al., 2024, Liu et al., 2025a]. The configuration sets a learning rate of 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}, momentum 0.950.95, Nesterov updates, five Newton–Schulz steps, weight decay 0.1, and gradient clipping at 1.0. The schedule applies 500500 warmup steps and cosine decay to 10−710^{-7} over a 15,00015{,}000 step global horizon.

The benchmark suite and evaluation metrics remain fixed. Deployment evaluation measures pass@1 with direct generation or execution success. Supporting diagnostics include pass@16, transition rates, energy, latency, and output length.

Reported Variation.

For the main experiments and training ablations, ±\pm denotes the sample standard deviation across the three independent training seeds. We first average each seed’s results over the complete evaluation set, then compute SD across those three means, using divisor 3−13-1. The selection-budget audit in Table E.8 instead fixes one checkpoint and reports bootstrap SD over evaluation inputs.

C.7 Hyperparameter Selection

The 27B hyperparameter search considers β∈{0.005,0.01,0.02,0.05,0.1}\beta\in\{0.005,0.01,0.02,0.05,0.1\}, λedit∈{0.0,0.05,0.1,0.2,0.4}\lambda_{\mathrm{edit}}\in\{0.0,0.05,0.1,0.2,0.4\}, and λstep∈{0.0,0.005,0.01,0.02,0.05}\lambda_{\mathrm{step}}\in\{0.0,0.005,0.01,0.02,0.05\}. Selection by aggregate validation accuracy under the three-seed protocol, with ties broken by minimized transition harm, yields (0.02,0.10,0.01)(0.02,0.10,0.01). These ranges describe model selection; the reported dimension ablations and joint candidate/horizon sweep provide the corresponding empirical sensitivity results.

Baseline models are instantiated under fixed matched settings. Standard preference optimization methods use minimal latency budgets; methods that operate on sampled paths consume longer outputs and higher latency budgets. LSPO narrows this efficiency gap by embedding machinery for local transitions into the parameters through answer internalization.

C.8 Reward Decomposition

The shaped path functional supplies the empirical ablations with a formal counterpart. Proposition 1, established in Section 2, shows that the progress reward telescopes into final energy improvement minus accrued edit and step costs, and Corollary 1 explains the preference for short, localized repairs over destructive global rewrites.

Telescoping identity.

Here TT counts executed Revise/Switch moves. A terminal Stop is a zero-reward self-transition and leaves the identities unchanged. Substituting the move reward from eq. 4 gives

∑t=0T−1rt\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}r_{t} =∑t=0T−1(E~​(st,q)−E~​(st+1,q))−λedit​∑t=0T−1d⁡(xt+1,xt)−λstep​T\displaystyle=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\big(\tilde{E}(s_{t};q)-\tilde{E}(s_{t+1};q)\big)-\lambda_{\mathrm{edit}}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}d(x_{t+1},x_{t})-\lambda_{\mathrm{step}}T (C.4)
=E~​(s0,q)−E~​(sT,q)−λedit​∑t=0T−1d⁡(xt+1,xt)−λstep​T.\displaystyle=\tilde{E}(s_{0};q)-\tilde{E}(s_{T};q)-\lambda_{\mathrm{edit}}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}d(x_{t+1},x_{t})-\lambda_{\mathrm{step}}T.
Corollary 1 (Preference for economical paths).

Let τ\tau and τ′\tau^{\prime} be two trajectories for the same prompt qq with identical initial and terminal states, satisfying s0=s0′s_{0}=s_{0}^{\prime} and sTτ=sTτ′′s_{T_{\tau}}=s_{T_{\tau^{\prime}}}^{\prime}. If

∑t=0Tτ−1d⁡(xt+1,xt)≤∑t=0Tτ′−1d⁡(xt+1′,xt′)andTτ≤Tτ′,\sum_{t=0}^{T_{\tau}-1}d(x_{t+1},x_{t})\leq\sum_{t=0}^{T_{\tau^{\prime}}-1}d(x_{t+1}^{\prime},x_{t}^{\prime})\hskip 18.49988pt\text{and}\hskip 18.49988ptT_{\tau}\leq T_{\tau^{\prime}}, (C.5)

then the cumulative shaped reward satisfies R⁡(τ,q)≥R⁡(τ′,q)R(\tau;q)\geq R(\tau^{\prime};q). The inequality is strict whenever at least one inequality is strict and the corresponding coefficient λedit\lambda_{\mathrm{edit}} or λstep\lambda_{\mathrm{step}} is strictly positive.

Path economy argument.

Under identical endpoints (s0=s0′s_{0}=s_{0}^{\prime} and sTτ=sTτ′′s_{T_{\tau}}=s_{T_{\tau^{\prime}}}^{\prime}), the net energy term E~​(s0,q)−E~​(sT,q)\tilde{E}(s_{0};q)-\tilde{E}(s_{T};q) is invariant across paths. Under this telescoping relation, R⁡(τ,q)−R⁡(τ′,q)R(\tau;q)-R(\tau^{\prime};q) reduces entirely to differences in cumulative edit and step penalties, favoring trajectories that achieve the same descent with fewer tokens altered and fewer transitions taken.

The difference in energy aligns formally with potential reward shaping [Ng et al., 1999]. The edit and step penalties restrict the preferred policy class by penalizing unnecessarily long or destructive correction paths, favoring economical paths with net energy improvement.

C.9 Noise Robustness

The ablation with noisy energy motivates a sensitivity analysis. Because the LSPO path reward relies on local energy differences, any bounded state perturbation results in a bounded endpoint error.

Proposition 4 (Bounded energy noise perturbs cumulative reward only through endpoint error).

Let

E^​(s,q)=E~​(s,q)+δ⁡(s,q)\hat{E}(s;q)=\tilde{E}(s;q)+\delta(s;q) (C.6)

with |δ⁡(s,q)|≤ε|\delta(s;q)|\leq\varepsilon for every visited state. Let R⁡(τ,q)R(\tau;q) denote the cumulative shaped reward computed from E~\tilde{E}, and let R^​(τ,q)\hat{R}(\tau;q) denote the cumulative shaped reward computed from E^\hat{E} using the same edit and step penalties. For any trajectory τ=(s0,a0,…,sT)\tau=(s_{0},a_{0},\dots,s_{T}),

R^​(τ,q)−R⁡(τ,q)=δ⁡(s0,q)−δ⁡(sT,q),and|R^​(τ,q)−R⁡(τ,q)|≤2​ε.\hat{R}(\tau;q)-R(\tau;q)=\delta(s_{0};q)-\delta(s_{T};q),\hskip 18.49988pt\text{and}\hskip 18.49988pt\left|\hat{R}(\tau;q)-R(\tau;q)\right|\leq 2\varepsilon. (C.7)

Endpoint perturbation.

By proposition 1,

R⁡(τ,q)=E~​(s0,q)−E~​(sT,q)−λedit​∑t=0T−1d⁡(xt+1,xt)−λstep​TR(\tau;q)=\tilde{E}(s_{0};q)-\tilde{E}(s_{T};q)-\lambda_{\mathrm{edit}}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}d(x_{t+1},x_{t})-\lambda_{\mathrm{step}}T (C.8)

and

R^​(τ,q)=E^​(s0,q)−E^​(sT,q)−λedit​∑t=0T−1d⁡(xt+1,xt)−λstep​T.\hat{R}(\tau;q)=\hat{E}(s_{0};q)-\hat{E}(s_{T};q)-\lambda_{\mathrm{edit}}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}d(x_{t+1},x_{t})-\lambda_{\mathrm{step}}T. (C.9)

Subtracting the two expressions cancels the penalty terms and leaves

R^​(τ,q)−R⁡(τ,q)=δ⁡(s0,q)−δ⁡(sT,q).\hat{R}(\tau;q)-R(\tau;q)=\delta(s_{0};q)-\delta(s_{T};q). (C.10)

The bound uses |δ|≤ε|\delta|\leq\varepsilon at the two endpoints.

Corollary 2 (Trajectory ranking is preserved under a sufficient terminal margin).

Let τ\tau and τ′\tau^{\prime} be two trajectories for the same prompt that start from the same initial state s0s_{0}. Under the conditions of proposition 4, if

R⁡(τ,q)−R⁡(τ′,q)>2​ε,R(\tau;q)-R(\tau^{\prime};q)>2\varepsilon, (C.11)

the perturbed ranking satisfies R^​(τ,q)>R^​(τ′,q)\hat{R}(\tau;q)>\hat{R}(\tau^{\prime};q).

Ranking margin.

Because the two trajectories share the same initial state,

(R^​(τ,q)−R^​(τ′,q))−(R⁡(τ,q)−R⁡(τ′,q))=−δ⁡(sT,q)+δ⁡(sT′,q).\big(\hat{R}(\tau;q)-\hat{R}(\tau^{\prime};q)\big)-\big(R(\tau;q)-R(\tau^{\prime};q)\big)=-\delta(s_{T};q)+\delta(s_{T}^{\prime};q). (C.12)

Its absolute value is at most 2​ε2\varepsilon, giving

R^​(τ,q)−R^​(τ′,q)≥R⁡(τ,q)−R⁡(τ′,q)−2​ε>0,\hat{R}(\tau;q)-\hat{R}(\tau^{\prime};q)\geq R(\tau;q)-R(\tau^{\prime};q)-2\varepsilon>0, (C.13)

so the perturbed ranking is retained.

This bound gives a sufficient stability condition for a fixed candidate set under uniformly bounded state-wise corruption. The Gaussian-noise ablation provides a separate empirical sensitivity test. Applying the deterministic bound to any noise realization requires that all evaluated perturbations satisfy the stated limit.

Appendix D Internalization and Stopping Diagnostics

This appendix evaluates the alignment between training rollouts and direct policy execution, the step-level monotonicity of energy descent, and the formal mechanics governing stopping conditions and answer internalization.

Figure D.1 evaluates energy as an ordering signal. Across all three model scales, lower final energy is associated with higher correctness, though slopes and separation margins vary by capacity. We therefore compare absolute energy values within each backbone, consistent with prior work on model calibration and uncertainty [Kadavath et al., 2022, Yin et al., 2023, Guo et al., 2017].

Figure D.2 separates training exploration from deployed policy outputs. LSPO shows the smallest energy gap between selected training answers and direct outputs, the empirical signature of answer internalization. The analysis measures whether correction traces shift the policy distribution, complementing prior studies of self-correction [Kumar et al., 2024, Ma et al., 2025, Xiong et al., 2025].

Figure D.3 resolves the mechanism at the step level. The energy monotonicity rate measures how often a move decreases state energy; the rate of preserving correct states measures whether already correct states are retained; and the stop optimality rate evaluates whether generation ends near the empirical minimum along the visited path. The ordering of these diagnostics follows the geometric constraints encouraged by LSPO.

Figure D.4 extends the transition diagnostic beyond the primary 27B setting. The ordering persists at 9B and 35B-A3B. LSPO increases constructive conversions from incorrect to correct without the large conversions from correct to incorrect observed in search baselines with high cost.

D.1 Answer and Span Transition Metrics

For each method, answer-level transitions compare the before and after correctness labels of the same NN answer pairs. Let nW→Cn_{W\to C} and nC→Wn_{C\to W} count repairs (wrong to correct) and regressions (correct to wrong), respectively. Both reported rates use the full paired sample as denominator,

Gans=100​nW→C/N,Hans=100​nC→W/N,NetGain=Gans−Hans.G_{\mathrm{ans}}=100\,n_{W\to C}/N,\hskip 18.49988ptH_{\mathrm{ans}}=100\,n_{C\to W}/N,\hskip 18.49988pt\mathrm{NetGain}=G_{\mathrm{ans}}-H_{\mathrm{ans}}. (D.1)

Thus the 6.4% repair and 1.7% regression frequencies for LSPO yield a 4.7-point net gain. Correct-to-correct (C→\toC) and incorrect-to-incorrect (W→\toW) pairs contribute zero to this difference.

The span audit in Table D.1 uses before/after validity labels, denoted VV and II, for paired spans. Each method has its own initial valid fraction pVp_{V}. Preservation and damage condition on initially valid spans, while repair conditions on initially invalid spans,

Pspan\displaystyle P_{\mathrm{span}} =Pr⁡(Vafter∣Vbefore),\displaystyle=\Pr(V_{\mathrm{after}}\mid V_{\mathrm{before}}), Dspan\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{span}} =1−Pspan,\displaystyle=1-P_{\mathrm{span}}, (D.2)
Rspan\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{span}} =Pr⁡(Vafter∣Ibefore),\displaystyle=\Pr(V_{\mathrm{after}}\mid I_{\mathrm{before}}), NetSpanGain\displaystyle\mathrm{NetSpanGain} =100​[(1−pV)​Rspan−pV​Dspan].\displaystyle=100[(1-p_{V})R_{\mathrm{span}}-p_{V}D_{\mathrm{span}}].

Probabilities in this equation lie in [0,1][0,1]; net gain is in percentage points. Full LSPO preserves 95.8% of initially valid spans and repairs 29.5% of initially invalid spans, yielding a 16.0-point increase in the valid-span fraction. The matched no-lift control yields 9.9 points. These results support preservation and repair of the spans assessed by the validity labels; answer-level and span-level gains describe distinct units of analysis.

D.2 Stopping Condition

The stop optimality diagnostic has a formal counterpart. Continuing from a state cannot improve cumulative reward when every future energy decrease is exhausted by the associated edit and step costs.

Proposition 5 (A sufficient stopping condition).

Fix an input qq and a move index tt, counting Revise/Switch transitions. Suppose that for every admissible continuation

st,st+1,…,sTs_{t},s_{t+1},\dots,s_{T} (D.3)

starting from sts_{t}, each future transition indexed by u∈{t,…,T−1}u\in\{t,\dots,T-1\} satisfies

E~​(su,q)−E~​(su+1,q)≤λedit​d​(xu+1,xu)+λstep.\tilde{E}(s_{u};q)-\tilde{E}(s_{u+1};q)\leq\lambda_{\mathrm{edit}}d(x_{u+1},x_{u})+\lambda_{\mathrm{step}}. (D.4)

Every such continuation has nonpositive additional cumulative reward,

∑u=tT−1ru≤0.\sum_{u=t}^{T-1}r_{u}\leq 0. (D.5)

For the unregularized shaped return, stopping with zero reward weakly dominates these continuations. The action-KL penalty in eq. 6 can change the regularized policy preference.

Stopping argument.

The assumed inequality implies

E~​(su,q)−E~​(su+1,q)−λedit​d​(xu+1,xu)−λstep≤0\tilde{E}(s_{u};q)-\tilde{E}(s_{u+1};q)-\lambda_{\mathrm{edit}}d(x_{u+1},x_{u})-\lambda_{\mathrm{step}}\leq 0 (D.6)

for every u≥tu\geq t, i.e., ru≤0r_{u}\leq 0. Summing over u=t,…,T−1u=t,\dots,T-1 gives nonpositive cumulative reward.

D.3 Internalization Projection

The alignment figures motivate a formal interpretation of the answer internalization objective. Training selects an answer distribution with lower energy, and the deployed generator is then optimized toward it as closely as model capacity permits. For each input qq, hold fixed the sampled-target distribution μq\mu_{q} of selected outputs xT∗​(q)x_{T}^{*}(q) induced by the selection procedure during training.

Proposition 6 (Answer internalization as forward KL projection).

For each input qq,

𝔼x∼μq[logpθ(x∣q)]=−H(μq)−DKL(μq∥pθ(⋅∣q)),\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mu_{q}}\!\left[\log p_{\theta}(x\mid q)\right]=-H(\mu_{q})-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(\mu_{q}\,\|\,p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)\big), (D.7)

so maximizing JSI​(θ)J_{\mathrm{SI}}(\theta) is equivalent, up to the parameter-independent constant 𝔼q​[H​(μq)]\mathbb{E}_{q}[H(\mu_{q})], to minimizing the expected forward KL to the selected-answer distributions.

Projection identity.

Substituting 𝔼x∼μq​[log⁡μq​(x)]=−H⁡(μq)\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mu_{q}}[\log\mu_{q}(x)]=-H(\mu_{q}) into the definition of forward relative entropy yields the identity; averaging over qq and dropping the constant term gives the equivalence.

Proposition 7 (Bounded task scores are controlled by forward KL on the selected-answer distribution).

Fix an input qq and let cq​(x)∈[0,1]c_{q}(x)\in[0,1] denote any correctness or task success score for output xx. Define

Δq(θ)=𝔼x∼μq[cq(x)]−𝔼x∼pθ(⋅∣q)[cq(x)].\Delta_{q}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mu_{q}}[c_{q}(x)]-\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)}[c_{q}(x)]. (D.8)

The gap for each input obeys

|Δq(θ)|≤TV(μq,pθ(⋅∣q))≤12DKL(μq∥pθ(⋅∣q)).\left|\Delta_{q}(\theta)\right|\leq\mathrm{TV}\!\big(\mu_{q},p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)\big)\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(\mu_{q}\,\|\,p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)\big)}. (D.9)

Averaging over inputs gives

𝔼q​[|Δq​(θ)|]≤12𝔼q[DKL(μq∥pθ(⋅∣q))].\mathbb{E}_{q}\!\left[\left|\Delta_{q}(\theta)\right|\right]\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{q}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(\mu_{q}\,\|\,p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)\big)\right]}. (D.10)

Total variation bound.

For any function f∈[0,1]f\in[0,1],

|𝔼μq[f(x)]−𝔼pθ(⋅∣q)[f(x)]|≤TV(μq,pθ(⋅∣q)).\left|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{q}}[f(x)]-\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)}[f(x)]\right|\leq\mathrm{TV}\!\big(\mu_{q},p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)\big). (D.11)

Applying this to f=cqf=c_{q} gives the first bound. The second bound is Pinsker’s inequality,

TV(μq,pθ(⋅∣q))≤12DKL(μq∥pθ(⋅∣q)).\mathrm{TV}\!\big(\mu_{q},p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)\big)\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(\mu_{q}\,\|\,p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)\big)}. (D.12)

Finally, averaging over qq and using Jensen’s inequality for the concave square root function yields

𝔼q​[|Δq​(θ)|]≤𝔼q​[12DKL(μq∥pθ(⋅∣q))]≤12𝔼q[DKL(μq∥pθ(⋅∣q))].\mathbb{E}_{q}\!\left[\left|\Delta_{q}(\theta)\right|\right]\leq\mathbb{E}_{q}\!\left[\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(\mu_{q}\,\|\,p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)\big)}\right]\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{q}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(\mu_{q}\,\|\,p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)\big)\right]}. (D.13)

For each fixed target distribution, the bound links the alignment diagnostic in Figure D.2 to the training objective, showing that as the forward KL term decreases, the expected gap in bounded task success scores is correspondingly controlled. It conditions on a fixed μq\mu_{q} and is informative only where the generator can approach that distribution; thus, we use it as a consistency interpretation of the alignment figures rather than as an accuracy guarantee.

D.4 Comparison with Test-Time Reflection

Test-time reflection systems retain critique and revision within the inference loop [Jiang et al., 2026]. LSPO generates and selects training traces before deployment, then serves answers with the direct generator. The alignment diagnostics above measure how much of the resulting improvement persists in that generator, while the deployment comparison quantifies the cost of retaining deliberation at inference.

Appendix E Deployment Complexity and Held-Out Energy Ordering

Deployment cost, energy ordering on tasks held out from training, and compute accounting summarize LSPO’s operational profile. The diagnostics characterize energy as a local ordering signal and quantify the inference cost that remains after correction traces are absorbed into the model.

Figure E.1 quantifies the deployment cost of the direct policy. Systems that use extensive search can incur large latency and verbosity penalties [Chen et al., 2021, Guo et al., 2025]. LSPO produces slightly longer generations than standard preference methods such as DPO, yet remains below the token and latency costs of GRPO and SCoRe. The method stays within a practical deployment range while preserving the accuracy gains reported in the main text.

The next analyses study the relationship between state energy and empirical correctness. When lower scores correlate with correct outputs, the scalar can serve as both a shaping signal during training and a diagnostic of candidate quality. Prior work on calibration fragility [Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana, 2005, Guo et al., 2017] and semantic uncertainty [Kuhn et al., 2023, Farquhar et al., 2024, Kossen et al., 2024, Aichberger et al., 2024] motivates interpreting energy as a structural indicator of local state ordering.

E.1 Energy Ordering on Held-Out Tasks

The empirical correlation between low energy and correctness reported in Figure D.1 motivates a conditional calibration analysis. Under a shared prompt-wise monotone calibration map, an almost-sure energy ordering under a coupling implies an ordering of expected correctness.

All ordering metrics evaluate the utility score u​(s,q)=−E~​(s,q)u(s,q)=-\tilde{E}(s;q), where higher uu indicates lower energy and a preferred candidate under the learned ordering. The AUC between energy and correctness measures the probability that a correct candidate receives a higher uu than an incorrect candidate [Fawcett, 2006]. Spearman and Kendall compute rank correlations between uu and the binary correctness label over the evaluated candidate set, with Kendall using a rank statistic corrected for ties [Spearman, 1961, Kendall, 1938]. Pairwise preference accuracy calculates the fraction of differently labeled candidate pairs within each prompt where the correct candidate has lower energy, aligning with the standard pairwise ranking logic of preference models [Bradley and Terry, 1952]. The Bins metric partitions candidates into five equal-frequency energy bins and reports the length of the contiguous monotone prefix, measuring how many of the five bins preserve the expected decrease in empirical correctness as energy rises. ECE partitions candidates into bins with equal numbers via a frozen monotonic calibration map and reports the expected absolute difference between the predicted and empirical correctness probabilities [Naeini et al., 2015, Guo et al., 2017].

Data Separation and Locked Evaluation.

Table C.2 identifies the public training corpora. The main evaluation suites are MATH-500, AIME25, GPQA, LiveCodeBench, ZebraLogic, and MMLU-Pro. GSM8K [Cobbe et al., 2021], ARC-Challenge [Clark et al., 2018], BBH [Suzgun et al., 2023], HumanEval [Chen et al., 2021], and MBPP [Austin et al., 2021] provide additional benchmark-level holdouts for transfer and frozen energy-ordering audits. Both groups follow the same exclusion rules.

Domain overlap is permitted. Evaluation examples and near-duplicates are excluded from policy training, energy fitting, pairwise ranking construction, training-target selection, verifier/checker threshold tuning, hyperparameter search, checkpoint selection, selection of training and audit budgets, and construction of prompts, rubrics, or synthetic references. Use of other examples from the same benchmark requires explicit deduplication against the evaluation set.

Evaluation questions enter only the locked final evaluation. Generation and candidate selection use the fixed model and scoring branch without gold answers, correctness labels, test-time verifiers, or judge feedback. External checkers and judges score the resulting outputs for reporting. Decoding settings and the training budget KK and audit budgets KselK_{\mathrm{sel}} are fixed before evaluation; test results serve only to report performance across those budgets.

As reported in Figure E.2 and Table E.1, the domain shift reduces the LSPO energy AUC from 0.792 to 0.704 and pairwise preference accuracy from 0.734 to 0.658. Both metrics remain above the outcome only and shuffled controls, supporting energy as a local ranking signal beyond the fitted task families.

E.2 Direct Generation on Tasks Outside the Training Distribution

The evaluation on benchmarks held out from fitting also tests the deployed policy itself. The suites in Table E.2 follow the exclusion rules above, including exclusion from training-target selection. LSPO improves over Base on all five tasks and reaches an average of 74.9 on held-out tasks, above SCoRe at 74.3, without a regression on any task relative to Base. The held-out policy results complement the ordering audit: the frozen energy head retains local signal under shift, and the compiled policy transfers the corresponding improvement gains to direct generation.

E.3 Joint Candidate and Horizon Sensitivity

Candidate quantity and transition horizon affect the local candidate space explored during alignment. Here KK is the maximum total number of candidate states retained per input qq, including the initial direct-generation state s0s_{0}. Table E.3 varies KK and TmaxT_{\max} together under the same training and evaluation protocol, measuring sensitivity to their joint budget. The gain persists at every tested budget; aggregate accuracy reaches 71.8 at the primary configuration (Tmax,K)=(6,7)(T_{\max},K)=(6,7) and remains at that value for (8,9)(8,9). The larger budget increases realized path length and reduces the ratio of unique candidates.

Proposition 8 (Accuracy improvement under monotone energy calibration).

Fix a prompt qq and two endpoint distributions μq,νq\mu_{q},\nu_{q}. Assume a common measurable nonincreasing map ϕq\phi_{q} calibrates correctness under each distribution, so that for κ∈{μq,νq}\kappa\in\{\mu_{q},\nu_{q}\}

ℙS∼κ​(correct=1∣E~​(S,q)=e,q)=ϕq​(e).\mathbb{P}_{S\sim\kappa}\big(\mathrm{correct}=1\mid\tilde{E}(S;q)=e,q\big)=\phi_{q}(e). (E.1)

Suppose there exists a coupling (Sμ,Sν)(S_{\mu},S_{\nu}) with marginals μq\mu_{q} and νq\nu_{q} such that

E~​(Sμ,q)≤E~​(Sν,q)\tilde{E}(S_{\mu};q)\leq\tilde{E}(S_{\nu};q) (E.2)

holds with probability one. Then the coupled endpoints satisfy

𝔼Sμ∼μq​[ϕq​(E~​(Sμ,q))]≥𝔼Sν∼νq​[ϕq​(E~​(Sν,q))].\mathbb{E}_{S_{\mu}\sim\mu_{q}}\!\left[\phi_{q}\big(\tilde{E}(S_{\mu};q)\big)\right]\geq\mathbb{E}_{S_{\nu}\sim\nu_{q}}\!\left[\phi_{q}\big(\tilde{E}(S_{\nu};q)\big)\right]. (E.3)

Coupling argument.

Under the assumed coupling and the monotonicity of ϕq\phi_{q}, the pointwise ordering ϕq​(E~​(Sμ,q))≥ϕq​(E~​(Sν,q))\phi_{q}(\tilde{E}(S_{\mu};q))\geq\phi_{q}(\tilde{E}(S_{\nu};q)) holds almost surely. Taking expectations directly preserves the inequality.

The common calibration map and coupled ordering are sufficient conditions for the correctness comparison. An ordering of mean energy alone is insufficient. The empirical ordering audits assess local ranking utility and leave these distribution-level assumptions conditional.

E.4 Energy Semantics and Local Ordering

The energy E~\tilde{E} is a learned scalar head trained for state ranking. Unlike global uncertainty measures such as entropy or Fisher information [Shannon, 1948, Rényi, 1961, Fisher, 1925, Rao and others, 1945, Cramér, 1946], it serves as a local diagnostic of state quality, where lower energy identifies a preferred candidate within the immediate vicinity.

Recent evaluations of factuality in short form text show that empirical correctness depends on measurement protocols specific to each domain [Wei et al., 2024]. The scalar carries evidence here because it tracks constructive revisions within the transition geometry induced by LSPO. We pair energy analysis with transition diagnostics to evaluate both state ordering and answer changes.

E.5 Open Form Transfer

The open form pilot measures policy transfer on subjective tasks. We use the Literature and Arts subset of WritingBench [Wu et al., 2026b] and the Roleplay subset of MT-Bench [Zheng et al., 2023]. Each method generates one response per turn without revision or candidate selection, and the same judge model and protocol score all outputs. We also evaluate DRO-adapted, based on Direct Reasoning Optimization [Xu et al., 2025]. DRO optimizes unverifiable reasoning via token-level self-certainty rewards (R3), query-specific rubric gating, and variance-based filtering over GRPO. Because the original framework targets reference-based tasks like ParaRev, RaR-Medicine, ContractNLI, and FinQA, we adapt it to open form evaluation by supplying synthesized references and task rubrics.

As shown in Table E.4, training paradigms diverge sharply on subjective tasks. Standard RL with GRPO and self-correction with SCoRe degrade below Base to combined averages of 7.45 and 7.41, as optimizing exclusively for verifiable correctness weakens open-ended expressiveness. Preference tuning with DPO maintains conversational quality at 7.59. DRO-adapted reaches the highest combined average of 7.62 by leveraging rubric gating and reference guidance. Meanwhile, LSPO achieves positive transfer across both suites at a 7.57 combined average, clearly exceeding GRPO and SCoRe while remaining close to DPO. Crucially, while DRO-adapted depends on synthesized references and rubrics, LSPO operates in a clean direct generation regime with zero test-time references, rubrics, or verifier loops.

For a more local audit, we score seven candidates from the same prompt with the frozen energy head and use judge scores only as evaluation labels. We compute correlations within each input and pairwise ordering, then average those quantities across prompts. Table E.5 shows moderate alignment, strongest for instruction fit, coherence, and character consistency. Table E.6 identifies prompts requiring high creativity and playful improvisation, where the learned ordering is less reliable. Energy supports local assessment of constrained style and consistency; literary quality and expressive richness require additional signals.

E.6 Compute Disclosure

Training uses 8×8\times NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. The reported 2983.2 GPU-hours for LSPO is the mean cost of one training run across seeds 42, 1234, and 3407. Engineering evaluation requires concrete resource accounting alongside complexity analysis. Table E.7 documents the primary 27B hardware footprint and deployment cost in one view, including peak memory, elapsed time, total GPU hours, pilot budgets, latency, and output length.

The resource table fixes the balance between training and deployment. LSPO spends more during training than SCoRe, adding 117.5 GPU hours on 27B. At deployment it avoids explicit critique, revision, or search, reducing average latency from 13.12 to 10.93 s and output length from 1501 to 1265 tokens.

E.7 Energy Ordering under Increasing Selection Budgets

We audit how the frozen energy ordering behaves as the candidate pool expands around a fixed trained policy. The deployment results use direct generation (Ksel=0K_{\mathrm{sel}}=0); this diagnostic varies additional candidate generation while holding the checkpoint and scoring branch fixed. The evaluation-time budget KselK_{\mathrm{sel}} counts additional candidates generated beyond the direct output, giving Ksel+1K_{\mathrm{sel}}+1 candidates in the selection pool. For positive budgets, we select the minimum-energy state from the pool, including the direct output. The joint (Tmax,K)(T_{\max},K) sweep above concerns retained training states; this audit concerns additional generation after training.

For each evaluation input qiq_{i}, let 𝒞i​(Ksel)\mathcal{C}_{i}(K_{\mathrm{sel}}) be its candidate pool and select si⋆=arg⁡mins∈𝒞i​(Ksel)​E~​(s,qi)s_{i}^{\star}=\arg\min_{s\in\mathcal{C}_{i}(K_{\mathrm{sel}})}\tilde{E}(s;q_{i}). The energy column averages exactly one selected state per input over all NN audit inputs,

E¯​(Ksel)=1N​∑i=1NE~​(si⋆,qi).\overline{E}(K_{\mathrm{sel}})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tilde{E}(s_{i}^{\star};q_{i}). (E.4)

All inputs contribute regardless of selected-answer correctness. Energy and open-form score entries report means ±\pm bootstrap SD, obtained by resampling evaluation inputs with the checkpoint fixed. The SD therefore describes sampling variation over inputs.

Table E.8 reports MATH-500 exact-match changes in percentage points relative to direct generation, alongside absolute WritingBench Literature and Arts and MT-Bench Roleplay scores. On the 500 MATH-500 questions, the changes correspond to 0,+1,+3,+2,+1,−20,+1,+3,+2,+1,-2 correct answers relative to direct generation for Ksel=0,1,2,4,8,16K_{\mathrm{sel}}=0,1,2,4,8,16, respectively. Energy reductions use the fixed scoring scale in this audit. Increasing the budget continues to lower selected energy, while external quality peaks at smaller budgets and declines at the largest budget tested.

From Ksel=8K_{\mathrm{sel}}=8 to 1616, mean selected energy falls from 0.1950.195 to 0.1710.171, a 12.3% reduction, while MATH-500 exact match falls by 0.6 points and the two open-form scores fall by 0.05 and 0.06. These are observed changes in means. The continued decrease in selected energy alongside the decline in external-quality means at larger budgets identifies a boundary of the learned ordering under increased selection pressure. These observations qualify the use of energy as a local ranking signal over the evaluated candidate distributions.

Appendix F Qualitative Case Studies and Failure Modes

These cases translate the quantitative diagnostics into four repair regimes covering targeted mathematical correction, bounded code repair, preservation of correct local logic, and global backtracking.

F.1 Repair Regimes

The mathematics and logic examples exhibit the pattern measured by the transition metrics. Successful revisions change the flawed step while preserving surrounding correct structure. LSPO fits this regime, where the desired update is nearby and the energy signal can rank adjacent states.

The code examples highlight excessive editing as a distinct failure mode. RL over sampled paths can discover executable solutions at the cost of broad rewrites. The edit and step penalties in LSPO bias optimization toward economical patches that leave the surrounding logic intact, providing a case example of the tighter latency and output length distributions reported in Appendix E.

F.2 Global Search Failure Mode

Case 4 marks the principal failure mode. LSPO repairs nearby slips within a flawed path, whereas problems requiring exhaustive exploration may need a procedure that rebuilds a global search tree at inference. Geometric shaping is most effective when the required improvement lies near the current state, consistent with prior work on self-correction [Madaan et al., 2023, Shinn et al., 2023, Huang et al., 2023, Ma et al., 2025].

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The abstract and introduction present cost-adjusted transition credit, lifted-state learning, and answer internalization, with the primary 27B accuracy and deployment-cost comparison. Section 2 formalizes the objective, Section 3 evaluates it across dense and mixture-of-experts Qwen3.5 backbones, and Section 6 states its scope and limitations.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: Section 6 discusses dependence on energy-ordering fidelity, the local-repair scope, upfront training cost, and the current restriction of the auxiliary coordinate to textual deliberation and mainly verifiable reasoning tasks.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  11. 3.

    Theory assumptions and proofs

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  13. Answer: [Yes]

  14. Justification: The formal results are stated with explicit assumptions and proved in Appendices A, C, D, and E. The main-text equations (Equations 4, 6, 7 and 8) are accompanied by propositions and corollaries with complete derivations in those appendices.

  15. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [Yes]

  19. Justification: Appendix C provides LSPO pseudocode and the fixed seed set, objective coefficients, path-length limit, optimizer settings, and validation/checkpoint schedule. The public implementation and configuration are available at https://github.com/Venomrko/lspo.

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers, because reproducibility is important regardless of whether the code and data are provided.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

  21. 5.

    Open access to data and code

  22. Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?

  23. Answer: [Yes]

  24. Justification: The public repository at https://github.com/Venomrko/lspo provides the LSPO implementation, training and evaluation scripts, baseline and ablation scripts, dependencies, paper configuration, public training-data identifiers, and setup and execution commands. Appendix C documents the fixed experimental protocol.

  25. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

    • •

      Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).

    • •

      The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

    • •

      The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

    • •

      At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

    • •

      Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

  26. 6.

    Experimental setting/details

  27. Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

  28. Answer: [Yes]

  29. Justification: Section 3 gives the model and benchmark setup. Appendix C specifies the Muon optimizer settings, learning rate, momentum, weight decay, path-length limit, internalization weight, hyperparameter sweep ranges, selected primary configuration, seed set, and validation/checkpoint cadence.

  30. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

    • •

      The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

  31. 7.

    Experiment statistical significance

  32. Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

  33. Answer: [Yes]

  34. Justification: The main and appendix tables report sample standard deviation across independent training seeds 42, 1234, and 3407, with paired confidence intervals for selected controls. Appendix C defines how the seed-level standard deviation is calculated; the fixed-checkpoint selection audit reports bootstrap standard deviation over evaluation inputs.

  35. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

    • •

      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

    • •

      The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

    • •

      The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

    • •

      It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

  36. 8.

    Experiments compute resources

  37. Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

  38. Answer: [Yes]

  39. Justification: Appendix E provides a compute-disclosure table for the primary 27B comparisons, covering the GPU type, peak memory, elapsed time, GPU-hours, and pilot GPU-hours. The main-text tables and cost plots report deployment latency and output length.

  40. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

    • •

      The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

    • •

      The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

  41. 9.

    Code of ethics

  42. Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

  43. Answer: [Yes]

  44. Justification: To the best of our knowledge, the work conforms with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. It uses existing model families and publicly available benchmarks and does not involve human subjects.

  45. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

    • •

      If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

    • •

      The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  46. 10.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [No]

  49. Justification: Section 6 discusses deployment efficiency and technical failure modes, but the paper does not explicitly assess both positive and negative societal impacts beyond those technical considerations.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  51. 11.

    Safeguards

  52. Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  53. Answer: [N/A]

  54. Justification: The current release provides research code, but no new model weights, dataset, or public inference endpoint with a high risk for misuse.

  55. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

    • •

      Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

    • •

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

    • •

      We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

  56. 12.

    Licenses for existing assets

  57. Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?

  58. Answer: [Yes]

  59. Justification: The paper credits the model families, benchmarks, datasets, and prior methods used. The public repository identifies its training-data sources, notes that model weights and datasets retain their respective licenses, and releases the original LSPO code under the MIT license. Third-party model weights and datasets are not redistributed.

  60. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets.

    • •

      The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset.

    • •

      The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL.

    • •

      The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset.

    • •

      For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided.

    • •

      If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset.

    • •

      For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.

    • •

      If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.

  61. 13.

    New assets

  62. Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets?

  63. Answer: [Yes]

  64. Justification: The new LSPO software is available at https://github.com/Venomrko/lspo with an MIT license, dependency list, paper configuration, data-source identifiers, hardware requirements, and training and evaluation instructions. No new dataset or model checkpoint is released.

  65. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets.

    • •

      Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc.

    • •

      The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used.

    • •

      At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file.

  66. 14.

    Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects

  67. Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)?

  68. Answer: [N/A]

  69. Justification: The work does not involve crowdsourcing or research with human subjects.

  70. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper.

    • •

      According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector.

  71. 15.

    Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects

  72. Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained?

  73. Answer: [N/A]

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper.
